Butterfly

GeometryCirclesPermutations
Game: Lines cross a stack of circles and make a shape like a butterfly. Watch the place where the lines meet.
How to play: Drag M, A or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Change the number of circles, press Permute, then press Check the claim.
2
Look for the math

A butterfly looks like a drawing game, but one small length never changes when you move its wings. The surprise is that the point in the middle stays exactly halfway between the two places where the wings cross the horizontal line.

One circle: the plain butterfly

Take a chord PQ of a circle and let M be its midpoint. Draw two more chords through M, from A to B and from C to D. Join A to D and C to B; they meet PQ at X and Y. The butterfly theorem says M is also the midpoint of XY: MX = MY. With one circle on the page, the logic test checks this on hundreds of drawings and it holds every time.

Why the midpoint stays put

M is the midpoint of PQ because the line PQ is at right angles to the radius OM. For every chord AB through M, the two pieces on either side of M multiply to the same number, whichever way the chord is tilted: MA × MB = r² - OM². That is the power of the point M inside the circle. Similar triangles then give MX²/MY² = (r² - MX²)/(r² - MY²), so MX = MY. The test checks the product on both spikes of every circle.

More circles, any pairing

The applet actually shows the 2N-wing version: N circles share the center O, and two spikes through M cut circle i in Ai, Bi and Ci, Di. Pair Ai with Dp(i) and Ci with Bp(i) for any permutation p. If Xi and Yi are where those lines cross PQ, then 1/MX₁ + … + 1/MXN = 1/MY₁ + … + 1/MYN. The logic test checks this for all N from 1 to 10 and, for N up to 6, tries every permutation: the sum never changes. For N = 1 the formula says 1/MX = 1/MY, which is the plain butterfly theorem again.

What breaks it

The equality needs M to be the midpoint of the chord in each circle. The applet starts with M on the line through O at right angles to PQ, so that is true. Drag M sideways and it stops being true: the test checks that the two sums then differ. This is a feature of the original applet, not a mistake in the theorem. The original page prints the theorem and five proofs; the applet itself sits on its 2N-Wing Butterfly Problem page, while the proofs are on the Butterfly Theorem article.

Try one circle first and press Check the claim. Then set the slider to ten circles and press Permute: the butterfly changes, but the two sums still agree.
